stories.headline: Update: Iran Warns of 'Faster, Heavier' Response as U.S.-Iran Conflict Intensifies
stories.summary:
Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned Sunday of "a faster, heavier, and more painful response" to U.S. strikes, saying Americans must understand "before it is too late" that the "rules of the game have changed." The warning came as Iranian state media claimed the country's Navy attacked an American remote-controlled vessel attempting to enter the Strait of Hormuz — a claim the U.S. military flatly denied. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth reiterated that any Iranian attack on U.S. ships would result in the destruction of Iranian oil tankers.

The new development marks a material escalation in rhetoric following a week of renewed fighting after a 60-day ceasefire expired last month. The U.S. has launched multiple strikes on Iranian oil tankers, and Iran has retaliated against American targets in the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Jordan. The Strait of Hormuz, effectively closed since the conflict began in February, remains a central flashpoint.

The economic toll is mounting for American consumers: the average price of diesel in the U.S. hit $5.85 per gallon Friday, up from $3.71 a year ago. U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Sunday that roughly 9 million barrels of oil per day are now moving through the strait, representing about two-thirds of pre-conflict flows, which he said could help ease energy prices.

President Trump said this week the renewed fighting would not last "too long," but months of negotiations have yielded no lasting peace agreement, and diplomatic officials see little prospect of an imminent settlement.

stories.headline: Update: Israeli Strikes in Southern Lebanon Kill Nine, Including Child, as Ceasefire Frays
stories.summary:
Israeli airstrikes on the southern Lebanese village of Kfar Remman killed at least nine people overnight, including a child, a woman, and a paramedic, according to Lebanon's health ministry. One strike destroyed a three-story residential building, killing eight; a second hit a vehicle carrying paramedics, killing one. Eleven others were wounded. The Israeli military said it was looking into the reports; the Israeli foreign ministry accused Hezbollah of "repeated drone attacks" and attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in violation of the ceasefire agreement.

The strikes are part of an intensified Israeli military campaign in southern Lebanon over recent days, targeting areas near the strip of territory occupied by Israeli troops. Large numbers of residents have again been fleeing the region. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun condemned the attacks as a "dangerous escalation" jeopardizing the U.S.-brokered ceasefire reached in June and urged international pressure on Israel to stop.

The ceasefire framework calls for Hezbollah to disarm, Israeli forces to gradually withdraw from southern Lebanon, and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area. Lebanon was drawn into the broader regional conflict on March 2 when Hezbollah — backed by Iran — entered the fighting. The health ministry said the death toll represented "irrefutable evidence of grave violations of international law."

The strikes come amid broader regional instability tied to the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict. Sunday's strikes in Kfar Remman followed attacks the previous day that killed seven people across southern Lebanon.

stories.headline: Update: Anak Krakatau Eruption Strands 270,000 Passengers as Indonesian Airport Closures Extend Into Second Day
stories.summary:
The eruption of Indonesia's Anak Krakatau volcano has left approximately 270,000 passengers stranded after canceling more than 2,000 flights and forcing airport closures into a second day. Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and three other facilities extended shutdowns until 18:00 local time Monday after volcanic ash was detected in nearby airspaces. Schools in the region moved to online classes and some shipping operations were disrupted.

The volcano, located roughly 150 kilometers from Jakarta in the Sunda Strait, began erupting late Friday, producing lava fountains and sending ash as high as 15,000 meters on the Sumatra side. Indonesia's Geological Agency warned Monday that "the probability of further eruptions in the coming periods remains high." The eruption has affected travelers across the archipelago, with stranded passengers facing days-long delays and scrambling for alternative transport.

The scale of disruption has grown substantially since the story was first reported, with the stranded passenger count rising from 150,000 to 270,000 and closures expanding. A newly wed Malaysian couple in Bali was told the next available flight home to Kuala Lumpur would not depart until September 11.

stories.headline: China Injects $54 Billion Into State Banks and Insurers to Shore Up Slowing Economy
stories.summary:
China's finance ministry announced Sunday it will inject 360 billion yuan ($53.6 billion) into eight state-owned banks and insurance companies, including the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China and the Agricultural Bank of China. State news agency Xinhua said the move is designed to enhance the institutions' "sound operating capabilities, risk resistance capabilities, and ability to serve the real economy." The package marks Beijing's latest effort to reinvigorate the world's second-largest economy.

China faces a confluence of headwinds: a years-long property market slump, a shrinking workforce, trade tensions with the West, and the economic impact of the ongoing U.S.-Iran war on global oil prices. GDP growth slowed to 4.3 percent in the second quarter, below Beijing's already-reduced annual target range of 4.5 to 5 percent — the lowest growth goal set by the government since 1991.

State media outlet Global Times said the capital injection would give financial institutions more resources to channel into credit for the broader economy "while strengthening their ability to withstand external shocks at a time of global financial uncertainty." President Xi Jinping has repeatedly identified financial stability as central to China's national security.
